title: Standards (NS & IS) and tests for civil engineering materials
summary: This subchapter is almost entirely numbers and apparatus: which test measures which property, which instrument it uses, and what limit the standard sets. The options are deliberately close together, so approximate memory is not enough. The highest-yield areas are the cement tests (Vicat, Le Chatelier, Blaine), the brick tests (compressive strength, water absorption), the aggregate tests (impact, crushing, abrasion, flakiness, silt) and the concrete tests (slump, cube, non-destructive). Learn each as a triple — property, apparatus, limit.

sections.heading: The standards themselves — NS, IS and NBC
sections.body:
Nepal has its own **NS (Nepal Standard)** series, administered by the **Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology (NBSM)** under the **Nepal Standards (Certification Mark) Act, 2037 (1980)**. The **NS mark** on a product certifies conformity, and for some products — **cement above all** — it is **mandatory**. A consignment of cement without valid NS certification should not be accepted on site.

For most materials and design procedures, however, Nepali practice **adopts or closely follows the Indian Standards**, and the examination is set on them:

| Code | Governs |
|---|---|
| **IS 456:2000** | Plain and reinforced concrete — the master code |
| **IS 383** | Coarse and fine aggregate |
| **IS 1077** | Common burnt clay bricks |
| **IS 1200** | Methods of measurement |
| **IS 2386** | Tests on aggregates (8 parts) |
| **IS 4031** | Physical tests on cement (several parts) |
| **IS 516** | Tests for strength of concrete |
| **IS 800:2007** | Structural steel |
| **IS 1786** | High strength deformed bars |

The codes with a distinctly **Nepali** character are those tied to local conditions:

| Nepali code | Governs |
|---|---|
| **NBC (Nepal National Building Code)** series | Building design and construction |
| **NBC 105:2020** | **Seismic design of buildings in Nepal** — revised after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, replacing the 1994 edition |
| **NBC 202** | Mandatory Rules of Thumb for load-bearing masonry |
| **Nepal Road Standard 2070** | Road classification and geometry |

A standard mark is a claim about **conformity**, not **suitability**: NS-marked 43-grade OPC is genuine 43-grade OPC, but whether 43-grade is right for the work remains the engineer's judgement.

sections.heading: Tests on cement
sections.body:
Learn these as **property → apparatus → limit**. Confusing the apparatus is the single commonest error, because three of them are named after people.

| Property | Apparatus / method | Requirement (OPC) |
|---|---|---|
| **Consistency & setting time** | **Vicat apparatus** | Initial ≥ **30 min**, final ≤ **600 min** |
| **Soundness** | **Le Chatelier** apparatus (and autoclave) | Expansion ≤ **10 mm** |
| **Fineness** | **Blaine air permeability**, or 90-micron sieve | **≥ 225 m²/kg**; sieve residue ≤ 10% |
| **Compressive strength** | **70.6 mm mortar cubes**, 1:3 cement–standard sand | 33/43/53 N/mm² at 28 days by grade |
| Specific gravity | Le Chatelier flask | ≈ 3.15 |

**Standard consistency** is the water content at which the Vicat plunger penetrates to **5–7 mm from the bottom**; it is typically **25–35%** of the cement weight, and the setting-time tests are run on a paste of **0.85 times** that water content.

**Why soundness matters.** Free lime or magnesia hydrates *after* setting, expanding and cracking the hardened concrete. Le Chatelier detects the expansion from **free lime**; the **autoclave test** detects the slower expansion from **magnesia**. An unsound cement produces concrete that disintegrates months later, so the test is a durability check, not a strength one.

**Fineness is not simply better when higher.** A finer cement hydrates faster and gains early strength, but releases **more heat** and shrinks more. That is why **rapid hardening** cement is ground finer (≈325 m²/kg) and **low heat** cement deliberately coarser (with a heat-of-hydration limit instead).

**Storage.** Cement absorbs atmospheric moisture and **air-sets**, losing roughly **20% strength in 3 months, 30% in 6, 40% in 12**. So the strength of stored cement **decreases** — a favourite single-fact question.

sections.heading: Tests on bricks
sections.body:
Under **IS 1077** and **IS 3495**:

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Compressive strength** | **First class ≥ 10.5 N/mm²**, second class ≥ 7.0, third class ≥ 3.5; the code minimum class is **3.5** |
| **Water absorption** (24 h immersion) | **First class ≤ 20%** by weight (≤ 15% for classes above 12.5); second class ≤ 22% |
| **Efflorescence** | Not more than **slight** |
| **Dimensional tolerance** | On a batch of 20 bricks |
| Hardness, soundness | Field tests — a fingernail leaves no impression; two bricks struck together ring |

In the **compressive strength test** the **frog is filled with 1:3 cement–sand mortar** and the specimen is immersed for **three days** before testing, at a rate of **14 N/mm² per minute**. Filling the frog matters: an unfilled frog concentrates the load on the rim and gives a falsely low result.

Beware collections that quote water absorption as "0.15" — that is a **mis-typed 15%**.

**Modular versus traditional brick.** IS 1077's **modular** brick is **190 × 90 × 90 mm**, which with a **10 mm joint** gives a nominal module of **200 × 100 × 100 mm** — so wall thicknesses come in neat multiples of 100 mm. The **traditional** brick still widely used in Nepal is about **230 × 110 × 70 mm**, giving 115 mm and 230 mm walls. Always note **which** brick a question specifies.

Other facts examined alongside: about **500 bricks per m³** of brickwork, a brick weighs **3–3.5 kg**, and the **frog is 100 × 40 × 10–20 mm** on the **top** face, laid **upward** so mortar fills it.

sections.heading: Tests on aggregates
sections.body:
Under **IS 2386** (eight parts) and **IS 383**.

| Test | Measures | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **Impact value** | Resistance to **sudden shock** | **30% wearing surfaces**, 45% other |
| **Crushing value** | Resistance to **gradual load** | **30% / 45%** |
| **Los Angeles abrasion** | Resistance to **wear** | 30% wearing, 50% other |
| **Flakiness index** | Least dimension **< 0.6 × mean** | **25%** |
| **Elongation index** | Greatest dimension **> 1.8 × mean** | **15%** |
| **Soundness** (sulphate) | Resistance to **weathering** | 12% Na₂SO₄, 18% MgSO₄ |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | 0.6% preferred, 2% maximum |
| **Specific gravity** | Quality | 2.6 – 2.9 |
| **Stripping value** | Bitumen adhesion in water | — |

Note that **impact and crushing carry the same numerical limits but are not interchangeable** — an aggregate can be strong under a slowly applied load yet brittle under impact. The **impact test** was developed as the quicker field alternative needing no compression machine. For **weak** aggregates the **10% fines value** is preferred, because the crushing value becomes unreliable when the material crushes progressively.

**Shape matters as much as strength.** Flaky and elongated particles **break under compaction**, so an aggregate that satisfies every strength test in the laboratory can still fail in the road by changing its own gradation during rolling. The preferred shape is **cubical and angular** — angular for interlock, cubical so it does not break.

**Grading.** IS 383 groups sand into **Zones I (coarsest) to IV (finest)**, with **Zone II** the reference for mix design tables. The **fineness modulus** is the sum of cumulative percentages retained divided by 100 — a **higher** value means a **coarser** aggregate. **Fine aggregate passes the 4.75 mm sieve.**

**Silt content.** The **field sedimentation test** limit is **8% by volume**. The laboratory limits in IS 383 are by **mass** and quite different: material finer than 75 micron ≤ **3% uncrushed**, ≤ **15% crushed**. Both figures are real, so read which quantity a question means.

sections.heading: Tests on fresh and hardened concrete
sections.body:
**Fresh concrete — workability**, and the test must suit the consistency:

| Test | Suits | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| **Slump** (cone 200/100/300 mm, 4 layers × 25 strokes) | **Medium** workability; the site standard | IS 1199 |
| **Compaction factor** | **Low** workability, dry mixes | IS 1199 |
| **Vee-Bee consistometer** | **Very dry** mixes | IS 1199 |
| **Flow table** | Very wet or flowing mixes | — |

The **shape** of the slump is itself diagnostic: a **true** slump means a cohesive mix; a **shear** slump means a harsh, non-cohesive mix prone to **segregation**; a **collapse** slump means far too wet.

Typical slumps: **20–50 mm** road pavements and mass concrete, **50–100 mm** ordinary RCC, **100–150 mm** congested sections, **150–200 mm** tremie or pumped concrete.

**Hardened concrete — strength.** The standard specimen under **IS 516** is a **150 mm cube**, cast in three layers each tamped 35 times, demoulded at **24 ± 0.5 h**, cured in water at **27 ± 2 °C**, and tested at **7 and 28 days** at **140 kg/cm² per minute**. A **100 mm cube** is permitted only where the maximum aggregate size is ≤ 20 mm.

Indian and Nepali practice uses the **cube**; American and European practice a **150 × 300 mm cylinder**, and they are not interchangeable — **cylinder ≈ 0.8 × cube**, because the cube is more confined by platen friction. A grade written **M25 refers to the cube**.

**Characteristic strength** is the value below which **not more than 5%** of results are expected to fall. Hence the mix design target **f′_ck = f_ck + 1.65σ**, with σ ≈ 4.0 N/mm² for M20–M25 — so a mix for M25 must be designed for about **31.6 N/mm²**, not 25.

**Non-destructive tests**: **rebound (Schmidt) hammer** (surface hardness), **ultrasonic pulse velocity** (uniformity and internal voids), **pull-out**, **cover meter**, **half-cell potential** (corrosion risk). The **cube compression test is destructive** — a standard trap in "which is NOT a non-destructive test" questions.

sections.heading: Tests on steel and bitumen
sections.body:
**Steel — IS 1786 and IS 432.** The **grade designation is the characteristic yield strength**, so Fe 500 means f_y = 500 N/mm²; nothing needs memorising once that is seen.

| Grade | f_y | Minimum elongation |
|---|---|---|
| **Fe 250** (mild steel, plain round) | 250 | 23% |
| Fe 415 | 415 | 14.5% |
| **Fe 500** | 500 | **12%** |
| Fe 550 | 550 | 10% |

Notice the trade-off: **as strength rises, ductility falls.** In a seismic region a structure must **deform without collapsing**, so **Fe 500D** (higher ductility) is specified where both are needed. This is central for Nepal. Tests: **tensile** (yield, ultimate, elongation), **bend and rebend** (ductility), and **chemical composition**.

**Bitumen** — each test measures a distinct property:

| Test | Measures | Conditions |
|---|---|---|
| **Penetration** | Consistency / hardness | Needle, **100 g, 5 s, 25 °C**; result in 0.1 mm |
| **Ductility** | Stretch before breaking | 50 mm/min at **27 °C**; **≥ 50 cm** |
| **Softening point** | **Temperature susceptibility** | **Ring and ball**, 3.5 g ball, **5 °C/min**, falls 25 mm |
| **Float** | Consistency of **hard** bitumen | Too stiff for penetration |
| **Viscosity** | Flow resistance | At 60 °C and 135 °C |
| **Flash and fire point** | **Safety** in heating | Pensky-Martens; flash ≥ 175 °C |

A **higher softening point** means a **harder, less temperature-susceptible** binder — needed in hot climates against **bleeding and rutting**, while a lower one stays flexible in cold and resists **cracking**. Nepal spans both extremes within one network.

The trend is from penetration grading to **viscosity grading (IS 73:2013, VG-10 to VG-40)**, because viscosity at 60 °C — near the maximum pavement temperature — predicts service performance better than a needle test at 25 °C.

formulas.label: Water absorption of brick
formulas.note: 24 h immersion. First class brick: not more than 20% by weight.

formulas.label: Target mean strength for mix design
formulas.note: 1.65 is the standard normal deviate for the 5% fractile. σ ≈ 4.0 N/mm² for M20–M25, 5.0 for M30–M45.

formulas.label: Fineness modulus
formulas.note: Higher FM means a coarser aggregate. Fine sand 2.2–2.6, medium 2.6–2.9, coarse 2.9–3.2.

formulas.label: Flakiness and elongation criteria
formulas.expression: Flaky: least dimension < 0.6 × mean.   Elongated: greatest dimension > 1.8 × mean.

formulas.label: Cube versus cylinder strength
formulas.note: The cube reads higher because platen friction confines its shorter height. M25 refers to the cube.

formulas.label: Bulking of sand
formulas.note: Peaks at 20–40% around 4–6% moisture and is zero at full saturation. Batch by mass to avoid it.
